1.	No contract for the construction of houses in Calgary has been let to the Bow River Construction Company by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The company planned to build houses for sale to prospective home owners. The houses were to be constructed on the company's own account and therefore no contract for the construction of houses was involved. However, as it was intended to finance the project under the National Housing Act, the company entered
into two agreements with the corporation pursuant to section 4B of the National Housing Act. These agreements provided that:-
(a)	The company would finance the construction of the houses it planned to build under the provisions of the National Housing Act.
(b)	The company would construct the houses for sale at a price not in excess of a price fixed in the agreement.
(c)	The corporation would purchase from the company on the expiration of a fixed period after the date of completion, and at a price fixed in the agreement, any house built pursuant to the agreement that remained unsold.
(d)	The houses were to be offered for sale in the first instance to veterans.
The agreements mentioned above were dated July 25th, 1947, and November 4th, 1947. All such agreements entered into pursuant to section 4B of the National Housing Act are known as integrated housing agreements and the plan as "The Integrated Housing Plan".

1.	What method is used by the government in collecting statistics as to persons killed or injured by motor car accidents on the highways, drowning, level crossing accidents, fires in homes, and other causes?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
1.	(a) Statistics on fatal accidents are compiled by the dominion bureau of statistics, through the co-operation of the provincial vital statistics departments, from death registrations, on which the cause of death is certified by the coroner, attending physician, or other medical authority. All deaths where an accident was involved are classified according to the international list of causes of death and in addition to other cross-classifications are tabulated by sex and place of accident (whether in the home or in industry).
(b) In addition, each steam and electric railway reports annually to the dominion bureau of statistics, accidents in which the railway is involved and in which persons are killed or injured. (3)	other headings not pertinent to this question. The dominion bureau of statistics also

collects motor vehicle accident statistics from the authorities in each province having jurisdiction over such statistics. These show the number of persons killed or injured in motor vehicle accidents.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. member for Peel was good enough to give me advance notice of his question. In reply all I can say is that it is very difficult in the circumstances that now exist in a large part of China to know whether missionary activities as they have been undertaken in the past will be permitted in the future under the new regime.
The government has had some reports, both official and non-official, from the communist-controlled areas in China concerning the treatment of missionaries there, and also as to the conditions under which they are being permitted to carry on their work. These reports are not conclusive; in fact in some respects they are contradictory. Therefore I think it will be some time before we know how effectively missionaries will be able to work in those parts of China now controlled by the communists.
It might be of some interest to the house if I went on to state in a few words the steps that we have been taking in the last few months to look after the interests of Canadians, including Canadian missionaries in China.
As hon. members may know, there are about 850 Canadians in China at the present time, more than half of whom are in areas outside communist control. As the scope of the civil war in China increased and moved south to the Yangtze river it became necessary in our opinion to get in touch with Canadian missionaries, and other Canadians in the areas north of the Yangtze, to see what we could do to assist them in the emergency which had developed.
For that purpose, as early as January, 1948, Canadian missionaries were advised by the Canadian ambassador that it might become increasingly difficult for them to work in the areas north of the Yangtze and east of the western border of Hupeh, and that consequently they might think it best to withdraw, at least temporarily, from these areas. On November 1 the warning, if you like to call it a warning, was repeated by British consular authorities, and the Canadian embassy associated itself with it. Similarly towards the end of November advice was again given to Canadians in that area to withdraw. Many of them followed the advice and returned to Canada.
Eighty Canadians, who were anxious to return and who had not other available means of transport at the time, were assisted by the Canadian government by the provision of air transport. Apparently about 600 Canadians remain in the areas of China not under communist control, there being about 300 in west China and 150 in south China. This number

Inquiries of the Ministry includes a great many missionaries, and the embassy has kept in touch with them in order to render all possible assistance should they find it necessary to leave. The wives and children of our own Canadian officials, and the female staff, have already been evacuated from Nanking where conditions are not very satisfactory at the moment. The ambassador and the male staff, however, have remained at their posts in Nanking, and will remain there as long as it is possible for them to work there, so as to protect the interests of Canadians to the best of their ability.

I have seen this country divided and I have seen the olive branch of unity tossed hither and yon. Of his party he said:

When the house rose last evening, Mr. Speaker, I was dealing with the problems of the Medicine Hat area, and was discussing the development of the Bow river extension. I gave several reasons why this project should be completed with the least possible delay. One of those reasons was the cost involved. While that area must be more or less resettled, there are many farmers in it who have been waiting for years to be re-established on irrigated farms. In addition, many young men who moved to the towns and cities during the war years now find employment not so easy to obtain, and they are anxious to get back on good productive land. The government should complete the main canals as soon as possible, on both the Bow river extension and the St. Mary-Milk river project. When that is done the people of the area will believe that the government really means business.
The completion of this work will greatly benefit many ranchers and farmers in that area who are interested in the production of livestock. It will provide water, which they do not have at the present time. Some of the farmers west of Medicine Hat have been in that area for fifty years. I might mention two in particular-Mr. C. D. Ronan and Mr. Nils Stenby. These two farmers were among the
The Address-Mr. Wylie first to settle in that area, and for all these years they have been waiting for irrigation. It is about time the government showed that it really means business, by constructing these canals and dams.
I might mention the work done by Mr. A. P. Burns in connection with the Bow river extension. This man, who has been a resident of Medicine Hat for years, has taken an active interest in the development of irrigation in that area. It is now the duty of the dominion government to make its stand clear and to supply the financial assistance necessary to complete this project. It might mean a big saving to the dominion government in the long run, as well as the establishment of many farmers on a selfsustaining basis.
In this connection let me indicate what it cost the dominion government for relief in that area from 1931 to 1938. I shall refer to the Meek report, published in 1942, with which most hon. members are well acquainted. This is what the Meek report has to say:
During the severe drought years from 1931 to 1938, the relief expenditures in Alberta amounted to $51,968,585, including relief works, direct relief administration and medical aid. The total relief expenditures in Saskatchewan amounted to $134,230,046 during this seven-year period, making a total of $186,198,631 for the two provinces.
Food, seed, feed and fodder, including freight, were main items of expense. During the winter of 1937-38 some 488,000 tons of feed were supplied in the drought area of Saskatchewan, and 44,000 tons in Alberta. Much greater quantities would have been required had not more than 474,000 cattle been removed from the drought area.
After listening, Mr. Speaker, to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) extol the virtues of the Liberal party in his speech yesterday, I wondered what party was in power in 1937. Was it the Liberal government, or just what government was it? One thing we must remember, even after listening to the minister's speech yesterday, and that is that the farmers of western Canada in the drought area still remember the price they received for the 474,000 head of cattle. The amount which the dominion government paid was one cent a pound. I am not surprised at the reference of the Minister of Agriculture yesterday to the increased income of the farmer of this country. His speech, Mr. Speaker, was what I would term a good election speech. It referred to only one side of the case.
We all realize that the income of the farmers is higher today than it was in 1938, 1939 or 1944, but we also know that their costs are considerably higher. Unless you

The Address-Mr. Wylie compare the income with the cost, you do not get a proper result.

Perhaps they were, but it must be realized that the farmers in this country today are called upon to pay greatly increased prices for tractors as well as all the other things they have to buy.
Since the Prairie Farm Assistance Act was brought into force, it has applied in every township in Alberta east of our irrigation district. The exception to this rule was in 1942 when the average yield of wheat in that area was approximately fourteen bushels per acre. In every other year the Prairie Farm Assistance Act has applied, and this presents a still more cogent reason for an irrigation project in that area. Irrigation will mean much to the people there. I believe there is a possibility that irrigation would even change the climatic conditions. Farming is our basic industry, and farmers must be kept prosperous.
I have mentioned not only the increased cost of living, but also what the farmers have had to pay in the way of increased costs of operation. Taxation has much to do with these increased costs. This matter was dealt with fully and fairly by the leader of this group, the member for Peace River (Mr. Low). For this reason I shall not dwell on that subject. It is about time the government realized that some of these taxes should be discontinued. There is a sales tax, a luxury tax of 25 per cent and many other nuisance taxes.
As has been mentioned in the course of this debate, we also have a two-cent tax on soft drinks. This is another matter which should receive serious consideration. The other day I received a letter from the Shamrock Bottling Works, Medicine Hat, Alberta, explaining that the soft drink is traditionally a five-cent product. When you consider that a two-cent tax is levied on a five-cent drink, you realize that this impost is just what the member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) labeled it, an iniquitous tax. It is time it was removed.
There is one other matter to which I should like to refer, and that is the amount paid to the older citizens of this country by way of old age pension. This also was referred to by the member for Red Deer. The time has

come when the government should give serious consideration to increasing the old age pension. It is unreasonable to expect anyone to live on $30 a month today. I know that this side of the house will at least have the support of one member sitting on the other side; I refer of course to the hon. member for New Westminster (Mr. Reid). I am sure he will do what he can not only to increase the pension but to lower the age of eligibility.
Another group of persons who are really up against it today are the incurables. I should like to refer to a letter which I received the other day, part of which reads as follows:
I am a member of the Canadian Association of Incurables and am writing you to help us unfortunate incurables and try to get legislation passed to cover a pension for us.
I am forty years old, with a family of five children, unable to work, and without means of supporting my family, because of the fact five years ago I was stricken with progressive muscular atrophy. Medical men of Canada and Rochester cannot help me.
That is only one of the many letters of the kind that we receive. I think the time has arrived when something should be done for these people. I see that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is in his seat. I know he has a big heart, and I hope that when he brings down his estimates this year they will contain provision for assistance not only for incurables, but for our older people, and many others who are in need of help.
I should also like to refer to another matter that affects the southern part of our province, namely, the transcontinental highway. The speech from the throne contained a reference to this highway, but it was extremely vague. As a matter of fact, this is all that the speech says on the subject:
A measure for assistance in the provision of a transcontinental highway will also be laid before you.
That was the extent of the statement. Before the provincial election in Alberta, the Minister of Mines and Resources (Mr. MacKinnon) was out there doing a little bit of campaigning.

Yes, it was very little. It did not help a great deal; we admit that. But he was there just the same, and in Edmonton, on August 12, according to a press report, he had this to say:
Hon. J. A. MacKinnon said today that a trans-Canada highway is "an absolute necessity from the standpoint of the country's economy."
The Minister of Mines and Resources has just returned home from the Liberal convention in Ottawa and he will participate in the August 17 Alberta general election.

Mr. MacKinnon said an independent commission to select a route should be set up without "undue delay", and that the highway need not be near the United States border, even though it would help promote the tourist trade.
I realize the significance of that last paragraph. The minister was campaigning in Edmonton, and naturally was working to have the trans-Canada highway go through that city, whereas we in the south of course believe it should go through the southern part of the province. I must say this to the minister, however. After the conference with the provincial premiers and provincial ministers of public works that was held here in Ottawa, the minister suggested that perhaps the government would pay fifty per cent of the cost of the trans-Canada highway. My opinion is that unless the dominion government contributes much more than fifty per cent, we shall be discussing this subject for years to come. I think it is realized by all provincial governments that the dominion government must accept a greater responsibility for the construction of that highway, which would mean a great deal to this country, not only now but in the years to come.
There were some other matters, Mr. Speaker, to which I wished to refer, but I see that my time has almost expired. In closing may I appeal to the government to provide irrigation in the drought areas with as little delay as possible. I urge upon them that they not merely talk about the matter this year, in the event of a federal election coming along, but that they show us they mean business by making a start on the project.
I appeal to the government for an increase in the income tax exemption applicable to individuals. The present exemption is altogether too low, in view of the increased cost of living. I sometimes wonder how the working people can get along on what they are allowed to keep of their earnings.
Last, but not least, may I appeal to the government to give a substantial increase in the pensions to our older citizens, those who pioneered and prepared the way for Canada's development. I appeal to the government to do these things, not only for the benefit of the people of my constituency, but for all the people from one end of Canada to the other.

November	 1,721,000
December	 1,112,000
January	 4,082,000
The January total was no less than 60 per cent beyond the monthly rate required for our target of $30 million a year. The total for the first three weeks of February-$4,-893,000-suggests that this month will exceed $6 million. Already, only seven months since the first project was received, we have approved the expenditure to the provinces of more than $13 million.
The house will recall the broad outline of the national health program:
(1)	Federal grants totalling $625,000 have been provided to enable the provinces to make comprehensive surveys of the Canadian health scene.
(2)	To strengthen and extend provincial health services, federal grants starting at $16,495,000 will be available each year for public health research and public health projects; to train professional health workers, to help crippled children, to fight venereal disease, to control tuberculosis, to strengthen cancer control campaigns, and to promote mental health.

The Address-Mr. Martin
(3)	Great increases in hospital accommodation are being encouraged by annual grants to the provinces, totalling $13 million a year.
These grants make possible an additional expenditure of $30 million or more each year on Canada's hospitals and health services. This is almost as much money as was spent on health by all governments in Canada- federal, provincial and municipal-as recently as 1933. This program of federal health grants is twice as much on a per capita basis as the federal health grants program in the United States.
In recognition of the importance of the national health program, the American Public Health Association-the most authoritative body in this field in North America -paid formal tribute to it when that body resolved as follows-
-that the American Public Health Association extend its hearty congratulations to the government and the people of Canada for a step which makes the year 1948 memorable in the annals of public health on this continent.
Mr. Graham L. Davis, director of the division of hospitals for the Kellogg foundation, in a recent article in the Washington Post wrote:
Canada is outstripping the United States in its planning for an over-all national health program.
In Canada, as in this house, throughout the country, and everywhere I have gone since the end of the last session, the action taken by parliament, by the government, has everywhere received an enthusiastic reception. Provincial governments, Canadian health leaders, the average Canadian citizen -all recognize this as an historic advance towards good health. The chairman of the Saskatchewan Health Services Planning Commission called it a fine and courageous program. Dr. W. A. Magner, president of the Canadian Medical Association, called it the most important event in Canada's health history.
Apart from a few important federal activities, health administration in Canada is centred in the provinces. The national health program, being worked out in closest cooperation with the provinces, does not in any way disturb their primary responsibility for health services. The centralization of health services would badly serve the Canadian citizen. In working closely with provincial governments to raise public health levels, the federal government is careful not to disturb the proper dominion-provincial balance of health responsibilities.
Access to good health is a fundamental human right. It is a right that every government must guard. When it became evident that our provincial defences against disease


and ill health needed strengthening, the federal government backed by the house took determined action. But Canada's health services are a complex of responsibilities, sometimes exclusive, sometimes overlapping. Federal, provincial, municipal governments and voluntary health agencies-all are concerned with Canada's health. Mr. Speaker, I am happy to be able to say that all of the nine Canadian provinces are now collaborating in this plan for the nation's health, Quebec, being the last to come in, having agreed to participate on September 7. In acknowledging the speed with which this great enterprise has got into full operation, I should like-and I know I do this with the full concurrence of every hon. member-to pay tribute to my two deputy ministers; to Dr. Fred Jackson, former deputy minister of health in Manitoba, whose great experience and reputation in the provincial health field makes him one of the great figures on this continent in the work of public health, and who is the administrator of the federal grants; and to all the other officers of the Department of National Health and Welfare and all provincial organizations and agencies who have worked during the past several months with so much enthusiasm and effectiveness.
In my talks with the provincial ministers of health, in my conferences with their deputy ministers at the dominion council of health, and in public statements made in every province in this country, I have reiterated the desire of the government that these federal grants should be utilized as expeditiously and as efficiently as possible. In this connection, to indicate my recognition of the problems that the provinces have to face, I should like to quote from an address I made to the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons in November last:
It takes time to assess and strengthen provincial programs and this might prevent full and immediate use of the moneys available. When I asked parliament to approve the whole amount for this fiscal year I did so for a deliberate purpose-to indicate how anxious the government was to see its grants fully utilized this year if possible. This year's allotment of $30 million is our target figure-the amount of money that we believe should be expended to bring our health services up to desirable levels.
The provinces have done excellent work in planning and carrying out the health advances made possible by these federal grants to the extent that they were not prevented by the shortages of trained health personnel, of technical equipment, and of hospital construction facilities. I am happy to say that these problems are now being tackled energetically and with considerable success. The house and the country will be interested in knowing that 600 health projects have al-

ready been received from the provinces and approved by the federal government.
Mr. Speaker, when this program was announced last year by the then Prime Minister, it was emphasized that these federal grants "would have the added advantage of being fundamental prerequisites of a nationwide system of health insurance." Indeed, they represent the first stages. The new services being developed and the new hospitals being built with these federal grants are hastening the moment when in every province it will be possible to consider further action towards hospital and medical care insurance-for which, of course, the federal government stands ready to provide assistance, under satisfactory agreements for dominion-provincial co-operation. It is of interest to note that in a recent radio address the Prime Minister said:
It is up to the people and the government in each province to take the initiative in working out health insurance plans in line with their local conditions and their traditions.
This national health program was not merely the fulfilment of the proposals made by the dominion government to the provinces in 1945-46. We went much beyond them. The best proof of this is that $17,123,000 more money is available in federal health grants for the provinces this year than if the health grants contained in the proposals had been implemented. I shall list the major changes since 1945-46:
1.	A new annual grant of $3,500,000 has been added for cancer control.
2.	The professional training grant has been increased by $250,000 a year.
3.	Over a period of years the annual grant for public health research will increase to $500,000 in place of the $100,000 formerly proposed.
4.	The federal government has now offered -in place of low-cost loans previously proposed-to give annual grants totalling $65 million over a five-year period to help the provinces increase their hospital accommodation.
I now propose to give the house the highlights of what has been achieved so far under the new federal health plan. I cannot do more than outline what has been done, but with the agreement of the house I shall indicate in more detail some of the lines of achievement by tabling some of the main projects that have been approved. It may be helpful if I remind the house again that this program is divided into three sections. They are as follows:
1.	The health survey grant-$625,000 in outright grants.
The Address-Mr. Martin
2.	The hospital construction grant-$13 million in cumulative annual grants for a period of five years.
3.	National health grants-totalling $16,495,000 this year and later increasing to about $23 million.
All the provinces have well under way the health surveys made possible by the federal grants. The total amount approved by parliament for this purpose has now been allocated. The provinces have established survey teams which are taking inventories of their health facilities and services, as a result of which new programs are being shaped up for their extension and development. In these surveys the provincial health departments are receiving the fullest cooperation from medical associations and other professional and voluntary health bodies. From all sides the most enthusiastic support is forthcoming for Canada's health plans for the future.
One of the urgent reasons for these surveys is to determine provincial requirements for new hospitals. There are obvious difficulties and delays in the planning and building of hospitals, but the total amount of additional hospital accommodation now under construction or in the planning stage, with this federal stimulus, is greater than ever before. The hospital construction grant provided by the federal government is being extensively utilized, as I will briefly indicate. Quebec, for example, has already had projects approved up to one hundred per cent of this year's grant.
I am glad to announce to the house that in this fiscal year federal assistance will be authorized to help build hospitals totalling 13,000 additional beds. This is no mean achievement. This is nearly one-third of the total of 40,000 beds which in my conferences with the provincial governments, I suggested as the government's target for the current five-year period. To summarize, these projects cover new construction totalling 12,983 beds distributed as follows:
1.	Federal grants have been approved for construction representing 6,401 hospital beds of all kinds throughout all parts of Canada.
2.	Projects for 2,882 new beds are at present under review.
3.	Further projects will be submitted, I can now say, before March 31 totalling a further 3,700 beds.
With the permission of the house I should like to place on Hansard a table indicating the institutions that have received approval for beds in the amounts first mentioned.

To ensure that the progress now being made will be continued and that we will reach or surpass our target within the next four years, it is the intention of the government to ask in the coming year's estimates for the re-vote of any unexpended portion of this year's $13 million grant. The hospital construction 
grant is therefore cumulative, while the health survey grant is outright and the annual national health grants are on a continuing annual basis.
These hospital construction projects cover a wide range, from large general hospitals and hospitals for the mentally ill, down to small

rural hospitals and nursing stations. It is not easy to select from a great number of projects that are being approved under this grant more than a few typical examples. By March 31, at least four provinces-Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Alberta and British Columbia -will have submitted projects covering all of their federal grants for hospital construction.
I might, however, make note of one outstanding project to illustrate the operation of this federal grant. In Quebec the federal government has approved the allocation of $1,498,000 to assist towards the cost of a magnificent structure now building at Riviere des Prairies to house 1,269 mentally deficient children. This hospital, modern both in its concept of early care and training and in its design, should be unsurpassed in North America.
The action that is being taken by the federal government to help build new hospitals in every province is far-reaching. At meetings of the Saskatchewan hospital council in Regina and the Ontario hospital association in Toronto, I was struck by the unanimity among executive members and delegates on the tremendous encouragement given them in their work by this federal grant. The extent of this assistance is perhaps best indicated by these two facts:
1.	On a per capita basis Canada's federal grant for hospital construction is twice the similar grant provided by the United States.
2.	By March 31 we will have paid out in eight months a higher proportion of our hospital construction grant than the United States paid in two years after passing its somewhat similar measure.
With regard to the third section of our federal health program, the national health grants, I should like to review for the house the way in which these grants are divided and the amount of money set aside for each purpose each year, and the results that have followed from their being made available to the provinces.
1.	Professional training grant-$500,000.
2.	Grant for public health research-$100,000 this year but increasing to $500,000 annually.
3.	General public health grant-$4,395,000 in the current fiscal year and rising to $6,500,000 by 1951.
4.	Venereal disease control grant-$500,000.
5.	Grant for crippled children-$500,000.
6.	Mental health grant-$4 million in the current fiscal year and rising to $7 million a year by 1954.
7.	Cancer control grant-$3,500,000.
8.	Tuberculosis control grant-$3 million in the current year, rising to $4 million by 1950-51.
The Address-Mr. Martin
I have reminded the house of these figures, Mr. Speaker, because from the mere recital of these grants it is clear that the provinces are being given an almost unlimited opportunity to exercise their ingenuity and initiative in moving forward on all sectors of the health front. Where the provinces already had certain well-established programs, such as those for the control of venereal disease, mental illness and tuberculosis, we have provided specially ear-marked grants. Where the provinces had their plans already made or in the formative stage, as for cancer or crippling conditions in children, we have enabled them to put their plans into operation for the first time on a comprehensive scale across Canada. Where, for other serious illnesses such as rheumatism and arthritis, the provinces had not yet devised their plans of attack, we have encouraged them to develop projects on a trial basis for the control and treatment of these illnesses, while urging them to explore the best means of developing allout attacks. With respect to health research, we have provided special financial assistance to increase the tempo and the scope of research efforts.
I know that this is a detailed statement, but the house has been thus far extremely patient, and if hon. members will follow me now until almost the end of what I have to say they will see the unfolding of a story which I think has been unsurpassed by any federal state in the world.
(i)	Grant for Professional	Training-
$500,000. We are also stepping up the training of health specialists, who are essential to the success of provincial health programs. This shortage of health workers is without question the main obstacle to health advances. I need not tell this house that the finest hospitals, the best medical equipment that money can buy-all these are useless unless we have an adequate body of highly trained and professionally qualified personnel to put these facilities into full service.
The professional training grant is already achieving results:	public health doctors,
dentists, nurses, laboratory technicians, mental hospital attendants, sanitarians, research workers, psychiatrists-these and many other categories of professional health workers are now being trained under it. In addition, specialists are being given training from funds provided under the grants for cancer control, tuberculosis control, mental health and general public health. Under all these federal grants, 537 professional health workers are receiving training at the expense of the federal government. As a result of the expenditure of almost $400,000 in the current fiscal year we can expect large reinforcements for Canada's army of health and hospital workers.

The Address-Mr. Martin
The most notable training project now underway is one submitted by the province of Ontario for the expenditure of almost $200,000 this year at the university of Toronto to train mental health personnel, such as psychiatrists, psychiatric social workers and psychologists.
If any member of the house does not think that is one of the most important problems on which we should be engaged, let him come with me any time and visit some of these institutions in our provinces and see how badly needed is the kind of assistance we are now giving.
Another project for post-graduate training in clinical psychology, bacteriology and preventive medicine, is going forward at the university of British Columbia, and, as a notable instance of action making for Canadian unity, at the suggestion of the Department of National Health and Welfare the maritime provinces have met together and agreed to back a joint program for mental health training at Dalhousie university.
(ii)	Research in Public Health-$100,000 to $500,000. Besides increasing the supply of professional health personnel, we must bring scientific research to support the health services of each province. That purpose is now notably being achieved through the public health research grant, which starts this year at $100,000 and increases-as research workers and research facilities become available-to $500,000 a year. The initial difficulties in getting new research projects under way are now being overcome and it is now certain that the full $200,000 grant for next year will be allocated.
The public health research grant is financing a number of useful investigations. For instance-and I can only give some examples -there is a community research project in preventive dentistry to find the value of the application of sodium fluoride to children's teeth. In British Columbia, a wide-scale study is under way of 8,000 school children to determine the value of a simplified system to gather health and welfare data for each child. In Saskatchewan, there is a study on the nutritive value of milk. Radioactive isotopes are being used to determine the efficiency of commercial detergents and to study the contamination of certain drinking water.
A three-year study is now beginning at Connaught laboratories in Toronto on methods by which the infection of the polio virus spreads. Other public health research projects include research into certain causes of maternal and infant deaths and the gathering of exact and detailed statistics on the extent
and nature of illness in a typical Canadian community.
Through this and other grants of the national health program, new impetus is being given to Canada's expanding medical research program. The national research council through its medical division is continuing its medical research projects totalling $350,000 a year; the Canadian Arthritis and Rheumatism Society is preparing extensive plans for research, for treatment, and for education. A considerable program is going forward with the support of the medical schools, voluntary organizations, individual donors and private industry; a particularly notable program, about which I shall have something to say later, is also being carried on by the national cancer institute. Since the incorporation of this institute a little more than two years ago, an impressive total of fifty-eight individual fundamental research projects on cancer are under way in many of our universities throughout the country. I thought a list of those projects might be of interest to the house, and with the permission of the house I would ask leave to table a schedule.

I feel I may say that the new energy put into research by the national cancer institute and the national health program brings the money available for health research this year to an all-time record of more than $1,250,000. I believe this represents an effort that is as fundamental and integral to our life as any that we discuss at any time in this national parliament.
(iii)	Extension of Public Health Programs -$4,395,000 to $6,500,000. Besides the grants to train professional health workers, and to support research in public health, there is a grant for general public health, which this year stands at $4,395,000 or 35 cents per capita. British Columbia has already been allocated 90 per cent of its public health grant. Here is what this federal grant makes possible:	many provinces are extending
laboratory facilities by the purchase of new, improved and much needed equipment; no fewer than five provinces are establishing branch laboratories at strategic points; all the provinces are improving local health services by the purchase of new equipment, and by the addition of staff such as public health doctors, sanitarians and public health nurses; Quebec, Alberta, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and British Columbia are strengthening their district health units.
We are assisting plans for Quebec to immunize children in the province against tuberculosis with B.C.G. vaccine, and to extend immunization for diphtheria to outlying districts in Saskatchewan. Saskatchewan is also being assisted in establishing a very extensive dental health program. A provincial division of dental hygiene is being formed; more dental service will be given to preschool children in Saskatoon; six dental clinic units will be provided, particularly for the rural areas; and four stationary and seven mobile dental units are being fully equipped to care for 40,000 school children, as a result of the grants made to that province by the federal government.
Dental health divisions are also being set up in New Brunswick and British Columbia. Other projects made possible by this federal aid include new public health engineering divisions in Prince Edward Island and British

The Address-Mr. Martin Columbia; a hospital inspection division in New Brunswick; extension of health education in Saskatchewan and British Columbia; and the strengthening of city health departments in Vancouver, Edmonton, Regina, Saskatoon, Winnipeg and Saint John.
(iii a) Campaign Against Arthritis and Rheumatism. Hon. members of the house will, I am sure, be particularly interested in the campaign developing in this country against arthritis and rheumatism, two of the great cripplers. I am glad to report progress to the house in this connection. The first results of recent intensive efforts are beginning to appear. The Canadian Arthritis- and Rheumatism Society, formed in 1948 as a result of a conference the government authorized me to call of the provincial governments and leading Canadian authorities, has now firmly established itself. From the federal health grants, funds have been made available to this society backed up, as I say, by the nine provinces. I am informed by this body that the moneys available from this and other sources are sufficient for its immediate needs. As soon as it has completed its planning and organization work the society will, of course, require much greater financial support. This association includes the Canadian counterparts of that great English specialist on arthritis and rheumatism, Lord Horder, who came to Canada last year to assist in planning our attack and who will return again shortly to give the benefit of his vast experience.
These are some of the objectives of the Canadian Arthritis and Rheumatism Society to make 1949 a year of great advances:
1.	Provincial divisions are to be organized and local branches or campaign committees set up.
2.	Programs are to be shaped up for research, professional education and technical leadership for local committees.
3.	The first national campaign for public support, supplementing that being given by governments at all levels, is to be carried on later this year.
4.	The society's advisory medical board is preparing an over-all plan that will play a role in the Canadian health scheme similar to that of Lord Horder's plan in Great Britain.
I know this announcement will be received oy over six hundred thousand people in this country with great interest and acclaim, and I am sure that the house will follow with interest the work of this society and will endorse my determination to give it every necessary support beyond what appropriately, as a voluntary agency, it will ask from the people of Canada for whom arthritis and rheumatism are such major health problems. British Columbia is taking action against these diseases and Alberta, I presume with federal aid, will inaugurate a treatment program for sufferers from these diseases. The British Columbia division of the Canadian

Arthritis and Rheumatism Society has been allocated funds from the federal public health grant to purchase clinical and other equipment for diagnosis and treatment. I hope to see similar divisions established in every province and to see activity in this field on the part of every provincial health department. I have every confidence that this public campaign now beginning against arthritis and rheumatism will continue to gather momentum until it can match the magnitude of the challenge of these great crippling diseases.
(iv)	Grant for venereal disease control- $500,000. The house is already familiar with the federal grant for the control of venereal disease, which was instituted after the first world war and served as an example of dominion-provincial co-operative health action until it was abolished in 1932. The grant was restored in 1938; under the national health program the grant has been raised from $225,000 annually to $500,000. All of the provinces, of course, have programs to expend the original allocation; four provinces -Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Saskatchewan-have submitted projects to use all of the increased allotment; the other provinces are rapidly building expanded programs. Every citizen, regardless of ability to pay, can now secure treatment. Through this federal grant we are making penicillin available free in all the provinces and free treatment services are being greatly extended. From 1944 to 1948, the number of cases reported has decreased by 29 per cent. With the new measures being taken we can expect this decline to be accelerated.
(v)	Grant for crippled children-$500,000. The house will, I am sure, be interested in hearing what is being done with the $500,000 that was voted last year to assist the provinces in helping their crippled children. As a result of the federal grant there are encouraging signs that the provincial governments are giving more attention to the special needs of crippled children. Here are some of the developments fostered by the federal grant: New Brunswick is extending its provision for free examination and treatment; Quebec is establishing a new treatment centre at Cartierville; Ontario is converting the Woodeden Hospital for cerebral palsy into a year-round operation; in northern Ontario a new clinic will search out children suffering from crippling conditions and encourage treatment and preventive action; Manitoba is developing a rehabilitation program; Saskatchewan is setting up a new provincial health division for crippled children. All this-and this is important-

is being done as a result of the national health program announced in this house less than a year ago.
The federal grant makes possible the extension of services for polio victims in Alberta. It makes possible the purchase of new and modern equipment for three of the British Columbia hospitals that treat crippled children. In all the provinces an accelerated preventive and treatment program to help crippled children can now go forward in full vigour, largely due to the stimulus provided by this national health program.
(vi)	Grant for Mental Health-$4 million to $7 million. The problem of mental illness in Canada has become increasingly urgent over the past twenty years. It is a problem that challenges every political party and civilized man in this country, regardless of race or political affiliation, and it is in that spirit that I approach it.

I thank hon. members, because I think the house and the country will be interested in this statement. The fact that there are now 50,000 patients in mental hospitals in Canada is ample evidence of the magnitude of this problem and of its cost in loss of productivity and in human suffering. Mental illness is being countered in many ways. The mental health grant and, to a lesser extent, the professional training grant are helping to provide additional workers in the mental health field; the hospital construction grant is helping to remedy the pressing shortage of some 27,000 hospital beds for the mentally ill; and, finally, the mental health grant itself, which stands at $4 million for the current year but will rise to reach $7 million, is bringing invaluable aid to provincial programs for enlarging hospital staffs, for increasing treatment facilities and extending the work of prevention.
The impact of this grant on mental health programs already is evident. The latest scientific, diagnostic and treatment equipment is being provided in large quantities for mental hospitals, mental health clinics and psychiatric wards in general hospitals. Special X-ray, surgical and laboratory equipment, badly needed in many of the provincial mental hospitals, is now being furnished along with equipment for modern treatment techniques and for occupational therapy. In Saskatchewan, for example, this federal grant has already made possible the allocation of over $50,000 for equipment. In Quebec, the provincial program will be greatly assisted through the federal grant to the Mont Provi-
The Address-Mr. Martin dence hospital for mental defective, although plans have not yet been finalized to take advantage of this year's federal grant of $1,140,000 for mental health.
British Columbia has used a substantial portion of its mental health grant to equip the new Crease Clinic of Psychological Medicine, which will be when completed, among the most modern on this continent. Similar preventive and treatment services are being extended through the establishment, with the help of the federal grants, of fourteen new mental health clinics in Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. In the wider extension of these clinics and of all preventive measures, we see the promise that mental illness will be brought under much more effective control in future years. With this federal assistance, as every one of the provinces readily acknowledges, because it is a co-operative effort, it now becomes possible to make a direct attack on this disease that will progressively shift emphasis from custodial hospital care to modern diagnostic, treatment and preventive services.
I have reserved to the last my comments on the progress that is being made under the national health program to bring tuberculosis under control and to combat the ravages of cancer. I link these diseases deliberately because from our victories-when I say "ours", I mean those of the provincial governments, voluntary bodies, tuberculosis associations, this parliament and the people of this country who work in this field-our victories, I say, in connection with tuberculosis, can inspire us to greater efforts to conquer cancer. Of course, final victory over cancer can only follow great research discoveries, but there is much ground that we can win back in the years immediately ahead.
The number of notable projects under the tuberculosis control grant is too great to be noted in the time at my disposal. With the indulgence of the house, I should like therefore to place on Hansard for its information a brief summary of the major activities sponsored so far by this grant.

Projects Approved Under Federal Tuberculosis Control Grant, 1948-49
Prince Edwards Island. Free diagnostic x-ray service, clinical laboratory services, and streptomycin and other drugs have been made available to patients. A medical director has been hired to organize a field tuberculosis service and the provincial tuberculosis control division has been expanded through the addition of new staff and equipment. A rehabilitation program has been commenced, and assistance has been given to the maintenance of a mobile x-ray unit and to the provincial educational program.
842	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Martin
Nova Scotia X-ray equipment has been purchased for the Victoria General hospital in Halifax, to enable all admissions to be x-rayed. Equipment has been purchased for the Nova Scotia sanatorium at Kentville and the activities of the rehabilitation division of the sanatorium have been expanded.
New Brunswick. Provision for free streptomycin has been made in sanatoria and an x-ray developing centre has been established to assist traveling units. Equipment has been purchased for the Saint John tuberculosis hospital, the Jordan Memorial sanatorium, the Moncton tuberculosis hospital, Sanatorium Notre Dame de Lourdes and Saint Joseph's sanatorium; and for clinics at Saint John, Fredericton and Moncton. A physician has been added to the staff of the Jordan Memorial sanatorium.
Quebec. Four mobile diagnostic clinics and a permanent clinic at the Hopital Notre Dame have been established. Provision has been made for free streptomycin treatment to sanatoria patients. Equipment has been purchased for sanatoria at Montreal, Mont Joli, Gaspe, Three Rivers, Dorchester and Cartier-ville. Eighty-five physicians have been given lectures in the use of B.C.G. at the University of Montreal and aid has been given to the Anti-Tuberculosis League of Montreal.
Ontario. Free streptomycin treatment has been made available to sanatoria patients, provision is being made for all patients admitted to hospital to be given routine x-rays and the number of free chest clinics is being expanded. A mobile x-ray unit has been purchased. A rehabilitation scheme has been commenced. Laboratory investigations are being extended in scope and diagnostic procedures developed. The tuberculosis control staff of the province is being expanded and specialists from outside the province are being brought in for advisory services.
Manitoba. Provision has been made for streptomycin and other antibiotics or treatment not covered by ordinary sanatorium rates to be supplied without charge. Free post-sanatorium pneumothorax treatment has been extended. X-ray equipment is being installed in general hospitals. Rehabilitation services are being extended and facilities are being provided for the establishment, at the Manitoba sanatorium, of affiliation courses for nurses. Sanatorium, clinical and laboratory facilities are being extended by the purchase of new equipment.
Saskatchewan. Photofluorographic equipment is being purchased for hospitals and clinics. Hospitals and clinics are being assisted to take x-rays on all admissions and the mass miniature x-ray program is being expanded. Provision has been made for the extension and development of the use of streptomycin. The existing program whereby B.C.G. vaccination is given to persons exposed to tuberculosis is being assisted. Post-graduate training is being given to staff physicians and the present tuberculosis staff is being expanded.
Alberta. Free treatment has been extended to non-pulmonary tuberculosis cases and a free streptomycin service is being provided. Clinical x-ray equipment to extend diagnosis services to remote areas, and technical equipment for the sanatoria in Calgary and Edmonton have been purchased. A short training course for nurses has been established at Calgary and the provincial tuberculosis staff has been expanded.
British Columbia. The province has purchased x-ray survey equipment for general hospitals so that all admissions may be x-rayed. Provision has been made for free distribution of streptomycin. An occupational therapy scheme for outpatients has been set up under the Metropolitan Health Committee of Vancouver. Equipment has been purchased for the Vancouver unit of the provincial tuberculosis control division, refresher courses are being given


to various members of the division, and a study is being made of emotional and other factors related to the treatment of tuberculosis.
More than two-thirds of this year's grant for tuberculosis control has already been allocated for new or expanded provincial programs. Let me remind the house that in the last fifty years in this country the death rate from tuberculosis has been reduced by 80 per cent. In the past twenty years it has been reduced by 46 per cent. This is perhaps the greatest single achievement in our public health history. It is certainly a challenge and an inspiration to all of Canada's health workers. The objective of our tuberculosis program for the next generation is nothing less than the elimination of this disease as a major cause of death and illness among our population.
The provinces have shown great energy in moving forward to an all-out attack on tuberculosis under the stimulus of the federal grant, which starts at $3 million and rises to $4 million annually. Already four provinces -New Brunswick, Alberta, Saskatchewan and Ontario-have applied for 90 per cent of their first year's allotment. The federal aid makes it possible for all the provinces to extend the reach of free diagnosis and treatment, and to provide free streptomycin, often effective against this disease. They make it possible for new equipment to be supplied in large quantities, and for new staff to be trained for the provincial sanatoria.
Because of the federal grant, Nova Scotia, Ontario, Manitoba and Saskatchewan are now buying additional X-ray equipment so that general hospitals can examine all admissions. Ontario will be enabled to have every admission to hospital given a chest X-ray. Because of the federal grant, new mobile X-ray units are being established in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Quebec to help discover early cases. As a consequence of these federally-assisted measures, the number of chest X-ray examinations in Canada will be increased by one million a year! This vast increase in anti-tuberculosis activity means a larger number of cases isolated in time to prevent them from spreading their contagion to other members of their family and community. It means shorter stays in sanatorium, more cures, fewer deaths, and ultimately, I am confident, complete and final victory over an illness that at one time ranked very high among causes of death in this country.
What we have done and what we are now doing about tuberculosis, we can and we must do in the other phases of the public health field in Canada. Canada has good reason to be concerned over the steadily growing number of deaths from cancer. The house will recall that shortly after I became

Minister of National Health and Welfare, taking advantage of the preparatory work that had been done by my predecessor, the present Minister of National Defence, I called together representatives of the provincial governments, the medical colleges, the Canadian Medical Association, the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons, the representatives of public voluntary bodies, to determine what action on a national scale could be taken to co-ordinate activities designed to effect cancer control. As a result, this conference decided to establish the National Cancer Institute, with which the Canadian Cancer Society is now affiliated. The institute was provided with funds to sponsor a large research program of which I have already made mention. I want to pay my tribute today to men who deserve the undying thanks of this generation of Canadians for what they have done in the field of cancer.
History will record what the people of Canada owe to this institute and to those who brought it into being, particularly men like Dr. Blair of Saskatchewan, Dr. Richards and Dr. Boyd of Ontario, Dr. Simard of Quebec and others who joined with me and my officials in a determined all-out attack on cancer. This action was followed by my recommendation to my colleagues in the government that a special grant for cancer be included in the national health program- a grant not included, by the way, in the proposals originally made to the provinces in 1945-46.
I have not mentioned the names of all those who collaborated with us in this enterprise to form the National Cancer Institute, but I have spoken of Blair and Richards and Boyd. Dr. Blair died a few months ago in the prime of life from heart trouble, due to the energy put into his work on behalf of the institute and of cancer generally; Dr. Richards died likewise a few months ago of leukemia, due directly to his work in the treatment of cancer. Dr. Boyd, I am happy to say-and with his approval-has himself recovered from cancer because of early diagnosis and efficient treatment. He is an example of what can be done with an effective program for cancer control.
Mr. Speaker, we will not have fulfilled our obligation until every person suffering from cancer in Canada is assured of the same opportunities for a successful result as that achieved by Dr. Boyd.
Through the cancer control grant, provincial programs can now be strengthened immeasurably. Saskatchewan, with an extensive and excellent program initiated 14 years ago, already has been allocated its full cancer
29087-54J
The Address-Mr. Martin control grant, freeing provincial funds for other purposes, as, for example, to combat arthritis and rheumatism. In most of the provinces, great activity is now developing under the cancer control grant. For example, Prince Edward Island is establishing two free diagnostic clinics and providing free tissue service; New Brunswick is purchasing $50,000 worth of cancer therapy equipment; cancer control activities are being actively supported in Quebec; in Manitoba, the federal grant is partly financing free diagnostic and radiation treatment; Alberta's excellent program for free diagnosis and treatment is being supported. In most of the provinces, money is being set aside from this federal grant to support the research being carried on by the National Cancer Institute.
In every province plans are going forward to take full advantage of the federal grant for cancer control. Our objective should be to have available within reasonable distance of every Canadian citizen a detection and diagnostic service to discover cancer in its earliest stages and to direct the patient to a properly-equipped and well-staffed treatment centre. The establishment of such centres is already being encouraged by the federal grant and in this trend lies much of our hope for further advances.
I have made this summary, and taken advantage of the patience of the house, because I believe that the country is interested in this report. I believe it wants to know how this money is being spent, and with what results. But I would not want to leave in the minds of the members of this house the impression that these new developments in any way reflect on the efforts made in previous years by provincial heatlh authorities to cope with problems that are basically their responsibility. This is too important a matter for political criticism. I feel that I should tell the house that, whatever my disabilities may be, I have thrown all my energies and my offices into this plan because I think that no man in public life in the last quarter of a century has had as great an opportunity for public service as that given to me through my administration of this plan.
For many years the provinces have been struggling with the manifold difficulties that present themselves in the field of public health, and they have developed excellent health services. But rising costs, the increase in our population, the aging of our people- these and other factors have increased intolerably the weight of provincial health programs.
Because of this, the federal government, in view of its national concern for the health of the Canadian people, has provided

The Address-Mr. Martin financial assistance to enable provincial governments, within the framework of our constitution, to carry out better their health responsibilities. Behind our thinking in setting up this national health program was the conviction that the energy our people had shown in war could find full expression in peace through efforts such as this to open to every citizen new opportunities for good healh. On all sides there is evidence of unprecedented activity.
In all efforts to lead this country into an era of better health we can take encouragement from recent progress. Let us compare the period 1945-47 with 1921-25. What do we find in this quarter-century? General mortality has decreased 16 per cent, infant death rates are down by 51 per cent, and maternal death rates by 64 per cent. There are many other encouraging trends. There are also some disheartening figures, but the over-all picture is bright. This is strikingly indicated by the fact that life expectancy at birth for Canadians has increased by 5 years for boys and 7 years for girls in the brief period since 1931.	< t|
In all that I have been saying today I feel this house can discern, because of the constructive action it took last year, the true pattern of health progress. The national health program is the latest in an impressive series of major acts of the federal government, in co-operation with provincial and municipal governments and with voluntary health and welfare agencies, to widen in Canada the jurisdiction of social justice. In the working out of this program, the medical, dental and nursing professions, the associations of professional and voluntary health workers and-in particular-the ministers of health and the governments of the provinces have given invaluable assistance and encouragement, indicating their conviction that the federal program represents a major advance in the continuing evolution of better health services for the Canadian people. May I say by way of conclusion-and again I thank the house for its patience-

My hon. friends apparently do not appreciate the significance of this program to the people of Canada. The full potential of the national health program has yet to be realized. Our long advance towards good health, with the more rapid progress that this program makes possible, now brings us, for the first time, within sight of an age in which the Canadian citizen can be set free from many of the bonds of ill health that now restrict his creative and productive capacities. But there are many obstacles still to overcome. To every Canadian now goes the call to work with a good heart to lessen the dominion of disease so that the killers, the cripplers-all that withers and wastes human life, all that wars against happiness-will be made subject to science and human skill.
In our time we have seen governments increasingly concerned about conditions that

only governments can rectify. A transformation has taken place in our thinking: we now accept without question that there are ways to the future that only governments can open. There are hazards to human welfare that only the collective strength of the community of citizens can overcome. We have seen growing in this country the humanitarian conviction that no Canadian should be debarred from adequate health care for lack of money. For we have come to realize the truth that his nation's prosperity, and the welfare and happiness of its people, are inevitably inextricably bound up with this nation's health. This is no new discovery: this is the high concept of public service that has led governments, conscious of their responsibilities, to care for the health of their people. At this time, should we not recall to mind how well Disraeli, same 72 years ago, enshrined this truth in memorable words:
The health of the people is really the foundation upon which all their happiness and all their powers as a state depend. Take the most beautiful kingdom, give it intelligent and laborious citizens, prosperous manufacturers, productive agriculturists; let the arts flourish, let architecture cover the land with temples and palaces; and in order to defend all these riches, have well-trained armies and a powerful navy-if the population remains stationary, if it decreases yearly in vigour and in stature, the nation must perish. This is why I consider the first duty of statesmen is in the care of the public health.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened with keen interest to the previous speaker, the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). I trust he will pardon me if I do not follow his speech in detail. I am delighted to know that he is so keenly interested in his department, and that he is happily satisfied with its record, as he has given it to the house. I am glad to know, further, that, according to his report, the progress of his department is keeping pace with the general scientific progress this country is making.
May I first of all congratulate hon. members who have preceded me in the debate- whether I have been in agreement with them or not-upon the able presentation of the different points of view they have placed before the house. I would congratulate specially the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) and the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains (Mr. Demers) upon having ably moved and seconded the address in reply.
As this is the first opportunity I have had, perhaps I might be permitted to extend congratulations to the new leader of the historic Liberal party (Mr. St. Laurent), who assumed the prime ministership a comparatively short time after the convention of the Liberal
The Address-Mr. Rowe party. I know he brings to the House of Commons a splendid background of Canadian culture, legal training and high character. I trust he may have the good health to permit him to carry the responsibilities which must go with his being head of the government and prime minister of this great dominion.
May I also extend my compliments to the leader of His Majesty's loyal opposition (Mr. Drew), the leader of this party. He, too, has a splendid background of similar qualifications, involving legal attainments, experience in municipal and provincial affairs, and high character. I am sure all hon. members hope that in his youthful years he may have the health and strength which will permit him to assume greater responsibilities, as years go by.
I know all will agree that these two cultured gentlemen have brought to their respective parties satisfactory leadership; and I believe they will bring to the House of Commons those qualities which will be an enrichment of our parliamentary life in Canada.
The speech from the throne is a procedure in each session clothed with dignity. It is a dignified presentation. However, there is nothing very mysterious about it. The speech is cautiously written by the government of the day and with exacting regularity it is graciously read to both houses of parliament by His Excellency the Governor General.
Sometimes in our discussion of it we treat it as if it were something quite different. The one now before us is much the same as many others I have heard read in the past. It is full of generalities and excuses for what has not been done. This speech from the throne is more remarkable for what is not in it than for what is in it. It tells about one royal commission which has not reported, and which has dealt with matters the government should have decided. Then it asks the house to adopt a plan to name another royal commission to consider other problems which, if the government were not so tired and weary, it would undertake itself. Therefore I say that I see nothing in it of great concern, and I repeat that it is more notable for its omissions than for what it contains.
In his speech the Minister of National Health and Welfare stuck entirely and solely to his own department-and I am not surprised at that. Had I been he I believe I would have done the same thing, because I would have been prouder of my department than of some of the others. I am surprised that in the speech from the throne we do not
846	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Rowe find any sign that we might get away from some of the weaknesses the government has demonstrated.
All hon. members desire the prosperity, happiness and welfare of our people. But that is not achieved by legislation; it is not decreed by order in council. However, there are fundamental and basic enterprises in the country which are vitally affected by trade, by taxes, by centralization of power, and by a disregard of enterprise and thrift. And in the time left to me to speak in the debate I shall confine myself to these subjects.
May I point out at once that the crippling burden of taxation in Canada today threatens to stifle the thrift of our people, and is already showing signs of strangling domestic trade as well as hindering overseas trade. Despite what anyone says, that burden of taxation has raised the cost of living in the last year.
We are told that we have adopted a new form of budgeting. I am not just sure what it is called-cyclical, or-

maintopic: PROCEDURE IN QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY

maintopic: PROCEDURE IN QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
