speechtext:
Yes, someone says "sickening". However, it is a new brain-trust type of budgeting which permits the government of the day to take from the people what it thinks it can spend or save better than the people can spend or save for themselves. The government is probably saving it up-although they spent a good bit of it down in Digby-Annapolis-Kings and Nicolet-Yamaska; and there may be a general election before long. Some say it will be in the fall, and others say it will be in June. The general public is not sure when it will be. I think the government is afraid to go, and afraid not to go.
I do know however that 250 more men were named the other day to go out to investigate people with small incomes. They are to find out if the labouring man has paid his tax. They must find out if he has made his return -the hired man on the farm, the blacksmith, the merchant, the retired school teacher, the retired clergyman. All these are men and women who are having difficulty because of the high cost of living brought about by high taxation. They are having difficulty finding the money to send their children to complete their university education. Now they are hounded by more inspectors-highly-paid inspectors-to find out if the government cannot get more taxes. Little girls and young men working as waitresses and waiters in the hotels are going to have their tips taxed. Probably the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) tips more than many of us farmers can afford to tip. I do not know how they will strike an average because some must collect more than others. There is this continual effort to reduce what is left in the hands of the people by these devious methods of extracting money that the
tMr. Rowe.]

people have earned, in many cases money that they need. Last year the government took $670 million more than they needed, or $200 for every family from coast to coast.
When you stop to think of that, is it any wonder that business is falling? Is it any wonder that unemployment is increasing? Is it any wonder that our overseas markets are disappearing? I can remember how the party that now sits to your right shouted to high heaven when a sales tax of two per cent was put into force in 1920. I can still remember the tears that rolled down the face of the former Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), when the tax was raised to six per cent in 1935. The Minister of Justice of that time and the Minister of Finance said that the people could not stand that tax, that it would add to the cost of living, that it would add to the cost of a pair of baby's shoes or of the furniture needed in the home, that it would stop people from getting married. They thought that there would be thousands who would not get married because the tax was raised to six per cent. But now it is eight per cent. I am rather careful about making prophecies, even though some cabinet ministers are ready to prophesy when the next election will occur; but I venture to say that this government will reduce the sales tax before the next election, or perhaps in its present political desperation they will abolish it. They know that they do not need it. It will depend upon whether the election is to be in June or July or whether they will hang on to the last hour in the afternoon, knowing that they will never return.
Then we have the excise tax, which I believe was put into effect in 1942. I cannot say whether it will be abolished or not. I am not going to prophesy any more because one would have to be a wizard to prophesy what might happen when the brain-trust bureaucrats in the Department of Finance who direct the financial affairs of this country do not themselves know from one day to another. I would not be surprised if some day at eight o'clock the Minister of Finance came in and glibly, with a show of reckless assurance, told us that Canada's dollar is now worth only ninety cents. That would be just as much a shock to people in business as when it was placed at one dollar. Such tactics have strangled enterprise and have taken away our markets for agricultural and other primary products. That has been the result of maintaining our dollar at a dishonest value.
I do not know the inner workings of that department, but I know that many hon. members across the way do not know either. There are very few of those who sit on the front benches who know. I do not know yet why it

was done and I am sure that the brain trusters cannot give a clear explanation of why they recommended that it be done.
I am not going to enlarge upon the burden of taxation, because everyone in this country knows what it means. This country was not developed under high taxation and this country cannot expand under it. The people of this country cannot afford to pay the high rates of taxation in vogue. The government know that, whether they will admit it or not. It may not make much difference now because a few hundred million does not seem to be very much in the eyes of the present government. As they are going to be in office for only a short time now I suppose we can stand the inflationary tax structure that we have.
Canada is a strong and powerful country. No country in the world with the same-sized population has ever had the same resources that we have. During the war we showed what a virile people we were. Our people must be strong to have endured this type of administration as long as they have. I am satisfied that they can endure it for a short while longer. As someone said the other day, there is bound to happen what happened in the hungry nineties, in the emergency of 1911 and again in the emergency of the thirties. Each time the Liberal party got the country into a mess, the people called upon the party to which I have the honour to belong.
That is not just a glib political statement, although I heard a lot of statements last night which were quite glib. Last evening we heard a tirade from the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who I regret is not in the house at the moment. I have a high regard for him and I enjoy listening to him speak because over the years he has developed the rather happy faculty of being able by the use of a strong voice and experienced eloquence to convince himself and recklessly assure himself that all is well, whether that belief is based on fiction or on fact.
I listened last night with as keen interest as any fellow farmer of his could listen. I heard him tell us about the trade situation in Great Britain. I made some notes at the time but when I read his speech in Hansard I did not recognize my own notes. Knowing that Hansard never makes a mistake I shall not bother referring to them. However, I think I can remember the things that were worth remembering during the noise and bluster of a most eloquent effort.
Despite what the minister has said about our overseas markets I do know, as every hon. member in this house knows, that Great
The Address-Mr. Rowe Britain has drastically cut her imports of foodstuffs from Canada. She has drastically cut her importations of salmon. She has abandoned her importations of poultry and apples. She has reduced her timber imports to only a fraction of pre-war quantities. She has reduced her bacon imports to one-quarter what they were in 1943. She has reduced her egg importations from Canada to 62 per cent of what they were last year, and her cheese imports are the lowest in thirty years.
Not long ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that that will not matter very much because we can sell to the United States. The Minister of Agriculture told us that in selling our wheat to Great Britain for hundreds of millions of dollars less than we could get for it on the world market we were building up a stable market. I think these men should get together. Last night the Minister of Agriculture said that we had not lost anything. About a year ago the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) said that in 1946 Canada sold her wheat for $123 million less than she could have got in the world market, in 1947 for $229 million less, and in the first two months of the following year for $358 million less.
In a press release the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) is quoted as saying that the two governments have already agreed that their representatives shall meet again before the 31st July, 1950, to settle any obligation that the United Kingdom owes Canada under clause 2(b) in selling wheat for that much less. Whom are we to believe, Mr. Speaker? One minister says we are building up new markets in the United Kingdom. Another minister says that we have lost them but it does not matter because we have markets in the United States. One says it has made us money; the other says it has lost us money. I am not surprised that the Prime Minister found it necessary to take dancing lessons to keep step with the crowd around him.
Never in the history of the agricultural economy of Canada have we seen such a socialistic state-planning muddle. The situation is muddled and befuddled by one who claims to be a free enterpriser, but he is always looking over his shoulder to satisfy those who recently have been courting so closely that in the next few months, probably before the election, you will see the greatest political marriage Canada has ever seen. That is not by way of prophecy; that is only by way of warning. I want to say to my friends to the left, as I would say to any maiden who is looking at an old politician, "Be very careful whom you marry at the present time".

speechtext:
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that last night the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) went back to a time before the war. He went back before 1930, but his remarks were slightly different from the speech he made last year. He mentioned Bennett buggies last year and he did not mention them this year. I have never seen him make a more eloquent attempt; I have never heard him speak more loudly; I have never heard those behind him pound their desks more vigorously, particularly when they thought interruptions might threaten. There is not one within the sound of my voice, including yourself, Mr. Speaker, in your non-political position, who does not know that we have lost the British market. There is not a member in the house who can rise and tell me that we now have a market for as many farm products three years after the last war as we had in 1921, three years after the first great war, despite all the progress reports we have listened to this afternoon.
The Minister of Agriculture says he has been here for fourteen years, but so have I.
I know something about the policies of the party to which he belongs. I was amazed last night, despite the experience he has had, that he expected even you, Mr. Speaker, to believe that my party never believed in trade, that it never had respect for the provinces, that it never had trade overseas, that it was his party that championed the old, dusty, free-trade doctrine in the west and protection in the east until the radio came into being and the people of Canada knew that there could no longer be high protection in the east and free trade in the west.
We have the highest protective policy now that this country has ever had, an austerity program, not prohibitive protection but austerity prohibition. Thousands were put out of business. Ten per cent has been put on right across the board, not even in the form of the countervailing duty that the party to your right, Mr. Speaker, planned in 1930. At that time they planned a countervailing duty, and left the determining of our fiscal policies to Washington. I am not so sure that, when they planned to inflict a dishonest dollar on our economy, that was not planned in Washington also.
I should like to reply to the warnings of dangers that I heard in the house last night. Let me refer to 1921, as the Minister of Agriculture did last night. That was the time when the Liberal party assumed power. Three years after the first great war we were selling to the United Kingdom 255 million pounds of 

bacon. That was the market built up by those who never had any regard for trade. What do we find now? We find that, despite the fact that the Minister of Agriculture told the farmers of Canada that they could depend on Great Britain taking a stable amount of about 450 million pounds, he has recently announced that Great Britain will take only 160 million pounds this year. By all the signs of the times the deliveries will be less than that.

speechtext: Is that Canada's responsibility?

maintopic: PROCEDURE IN QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY

speechtext:
In 1921 we sold 77 million pounds of beef to Great Britain. In 1930, when the Liberal party went out of power and the Conservative party came into power, we were buying and selling Danish bacon over the counters in Regina and other cities throughout Canada. We were buying canned beef, 18,000 head of cattle in cans, to feed our own people.
Then let us take butter and cheese. In 1921, three years after the first great war, we sold over twice as much cheese as the right hon. Minister of Agriculture has been able to make arrangements to sell. Yet he is the great champion of trade, the great negotiator for agricultural products, the man who has taken unto himself more authority than any other minister has since confederation, the man who can tell you what to sow and who can tell you what to reap, the man who sum-merfallows the farms one year and summer-fallows the farmers the next, the man who has cost the western provinces $300 million to $500 million. If there should have been any cost to anybody in Canada by reason of such muddling because of inexperience, then the cost should have been spread over the whole dominion and not imposed on one class of our people. I know whereof I speak. I do not pretend to be able to say it with the force that was evidenced last night, but for anyone to stand up in this house, let alone a man who has been here for fourteen years, and say that the overseas markets are developed now, and that they were hindered in 1932 by the imperial trade agreements, is something which I could describe but not in parliamentary language.
Not only had we lost our overseas market for mixed farm products, but every elevator in Canada was filled with unsold grain. The Minister of Agriculture led us to believe that he could make these people pay whatever was asked for wheat, and that we would always find a market for our wheat. What happened? The Liberal party negotiated more trade treaties between 1926 and 1930 than any other party has in a similar number of years. They bragged about the number of treaties they negotiated, and yet we find our markets

are steadily slipping away. Now we have a repetition of the old song, "twenty-one years is a long, long time." It is a long time since 1921. Canada has made some progress. It is very fine to get up and say we sold ten million dollars' worth in 1928 and that we sell only four hundred million dollars' worth now. That does not mean anything more than a woman saying that in 1929 she bought a better hat for $1.98 than she bought last week for $19.70. You do not compare things that way. If you do, why is our dollar today worth only about fifty cents or one-half of its former value?
As I have said before, Mr. Speaker, we must now face the stark facts. It is no longer fiction as far as the apple growers of the Annapolis valley are concerned. It is no longer fiction as far as the mixed farmers are concerned; and when this government get through "margarining" the dairy industry it will no longer be fiction to them either, when they find they have lost their markets for cheese and other products. I say the hour has struck, and this government should stop, look and listen. I do not want to be unduly critical, and I am not easily alarmed, but never in all my experience have I seen such a fiasco as our negotiations with the United Kingdom. If anyone has any doubt of that, just look at what happened. If those negotiations had been successful the right hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) would have referred to them in very different terms, and would have told us what had happened.
As a kindness to the minister, and in order to help him out, I want to try to explain to the house where I think we have fallen down to a great extent. For many years, both before and after I entered this house, we had those who wanted us to think there was something mysterious about the party of which the minister was speaking last night. On one occasion the Right Hon. Mr. Bennett happened to say that we would blast our way into the markets of the world. That was just a figure of speech; I have heard worse many times from the other side of the house, from both the front and the back benches. What he meant, as he often explained, was that we would try to get those markets, by buying more of their goods, by making trade agreements, or in other ways. The old, historic Liberal party is the one that was in existence, Mr. Speaker, about the time you came into public life. It is not the one that is veering toward socialism, with all these novel doctrines of state planning. It is not the party we see today picking up all the tag ends of other groups who are beginning to lose their identity. It was the old party that believed in free trade, who said, "If we want to sell our products in foreign markets they
The Address-Mr. Rowe must be able to buy." In those days we who came from the province of Ontario were regarded almost as enemies of the state because we believed in a fiscal policy which would give reasonable protection, which would provide full dinner pails for the workmen who made agricultural implements for use by our own farmers. Why, those sitting on the government side in those days thought you had almost economic horns if you even mentioned protection. Yet within about three years they brought in what were called countervailing duties. I am not surprised that some hon. gentlemen to your right look astonished, and do not understand what that means. The government which brought them in did not understand them either, until it was pointed out by the then leader of this party that this was a new form of Liberal free trade which from that time on would be amended in Washington, so that whenever Washington put on a tariff of fifty per cent we would increase our tariff to fifty per cent also. As a result we had the highest form of protection ever known in this country.
These doctrines are old now, Mr. Speaker, and perhaps it is unnecessary to talk about them. Even the party to your right have forgotten about them, though by devious means they have maintained the highest protection policy this country has ever known. How my friends to my left can support and love them just the same is beyond the comprehension of those of us who used to be condemned for suggesting reasonable protection. We were asked, "How can you hope to build industries in Ontario and Quebec? How can you hope to make the implements the farmers use if we are to sell in the British market, the greatest market in the world? We must buy from the British market if we hope to sell in it." How many of us have heard that argument. I have heard it ever since I used to go with my father to political meetings. From a fiscal tariff point of view, Mr. Speaker, if the party to your right did not believe that, they did not believe anything.
But have they been consistent in that regard? Even though it was necessary, because of the financial folly of trying to maintain a dishonest dollar, to establish an austerity prohibition policy with respect to United States goods, there was no reason why we could not have bought more British goods. As everyone knows, we were short of iron and steel, to the point we expected to have steel rationing. We were short of implements and instruments. We were short of coal. We bought millions of dollars' worth of coal from the United States, and though the United Kingdom increased its coal production last year fifteen times, Canada imported only about one-seventh of her imports in 1938.
850	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Rowe Even though we needed iron and steel hardware and implements, instruments and all the rest of it, we reduced our imports from Britain in 1948 as compared with 1947, despite the fact that the United Kingdom increased her exports to foreign countries by over twenty per cent. We took only one per cent of Britain's production. They greatly increased their exports to Finland, to Sweden, to Spain, to Denmark, to Czechoslovakia, to Poland and to the Netherlands.
Now that the party to your right, Mr. Speaker, seems to be losing confidence in its own policies, I am beginning to think they might have had something when they said that if you want to sell in a market you must enable those people to buy from you. What has happened in Britain? We find that Britain has made forty bilateral trade agreements with foreign countries, under which she has shipped her coal, iron and steel to Russia, the Netherlands, Poland and other countries, whether under the barter system or some other system. But we find that these great champions of trade promotion here, who have made one hundred and twenty-two trade agreements with the United Kingdom since the beginning of the war, are all washed up now except for three agreements other than that with respect to wheat. The one for bacon, as I say, was reduced to one quarter of what it was, and the other contract for eggs was reduced to 62 per cent of what it was. The quota for cheese has been reduced to the lowest amount we have shipped to Britain in over thirty years. We have followed this course after making one hundred and twenty-two agreements with Britain, but we were making them for one year, not for two years. Three or four of these agreements were made for two years.
I sometimes wonder, Mr. Speaker-

speechtext:
I thank you for the courtesy extended to me, Mr. Speaker, although I do not want to copy the weaknesses of the cabinet ministers and speak too long. Since it is close to six o'clock it would spoil a speech to commence it now, so I will continue for a few minutes.
Like the previous speaker, I feel this is of prime importance and I say it with all the sincerity I possess. If this great agricultural country of Canada loses the United Kingdom market, which has been our best market since confederation, then I say it will be a calamity for the Canadian farmer, the fruit producer as well as the wheat producer. In his speech last night the Minister of Agriculture did not tell this house why he lost those markets. He did not tell this house that the markets for which he had been paying so much are now being given to foreign countries. He did say that when he was in England he saw the reason why we could not sell apples from the Annapolis valley. He should have told the people before the Digby-Annapolis-Kings by-election. It remained for the newly elected member for that riding to tell the truth about that. The minister told us that when he was in England he saw every tree loaded with apples. Every apple tree in Britain seemed to be bearing more apples than ever before. Everywhere the minister went, he saw apples. He tried to impress the house with the fact that he did not eat anything but applesauce while he was in Britain. It was for this reason he was unable to sell apples.
I thought this was rather strange. Everyone in this house believed Britain was not importing many apples because the apple trees in Britain were loaded with fruit. We believed the British people did not need to import apples. I wanted to make sure the source of my information was correit, so I secured a copy of the Trade and Navigation Report of the United Kingdom, tabled in the British House of Commons on January 22.
I believe this information, Mr. Speaker, more or less justifies the statement I have made about the noise and fiction of last night's speech replacing facts. Last year the United Kingdom imported 466,179 hundredweight more of apples than the year before. Great Britain imported more than a million hundredweight from Australia. Importations from New Zealand the year before had been nil, but in 1948 they imported 357,529 hundredweight. From other British countries, Great

Britain imported eighteen times as many apples in 1948 as she did in 1947. From other foreign countries, Mr. Speaker, Britain imported almost four times as many, 121,945 hundredweight in 1947 and 471,883 hundredweight in 1948. In other words, Great Britain imported 466,179 hundredweight more apples and yet Canada, who exported 663,145 hundredweight in 1947, is today spending several million dollars in uprooting the trees. We have not exported a single hundredweight.
When you realize that Great Britain imported 23-5 per cent more apples in 1948, it seems highly unfair to inflict this story on us. I have just mentioned a few of the things the minister should have told this house last night as to why we lost the United Kingdom market. It is because we did not buy from Britain some of the goods that were in short supply in Canada. At one time I was cruel enough to suggest that the Minister of Agriculture would make a better minister of politics. Since we are both interested in agriculture, however, I should like to suggest now that he would make a better minister of applesauce' than of agriculture.
I realize that the empire trade agreements have always been matters to which those gentlemen to your right, Mr. Speaker, like to refer. I remember being in the house at the time these agreements were being discussed. I can remember many of the speeches that were made. When I heard the Minister of Agriculture mention that as a reason why Canada could not get into the United Kingdom market-well, that is too fast for me. I do not need to even refer to such a ridiculous statement during the few minutes so courteously allotted to me. I should like to say, however, that at the time the empire trade agreements were being discussed the exMinister of Finance and former member for Digby-Annapolis-Kings was in this house. I well recall the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett challenging him to vote against the empire trade agreements. He knew what those trade agreements would mean to the apple growers of the Annapolis valley, and when the vote came he stood up courageously as the only Liberal in this house who voted for the empire trade agreements. Mr. Ilsley is gone, Mr. Speaker, and the preference for Annapolis valley apples is gone too. So far as the government is concerned, the party to your right, Mr. Speaker, is gone too. So we see, Mr. Speaker, that the truth will out in time. I have said that you cannot bring prosperity by legislation, nor can you obtain happiness by order in council. But I believe-and I am glad there are in this country many people who still believe-that by hard work, enter-
The Address-Mr. Rowe prise, initiative, genius and the skill of our people we can overcome these difficulties.
I shall not, as had been my intention, take further time of the house to deal with centralization as it affects individual enterprise and initiative. But I could not help thinking about what the minister said last night when he was speaking about provincial rights. He waxed eloquent, stood out near the mace so everyone would be impressed, and said that the party to your left, Mr. Speaker, were now provincial-righters, that they had never stood for provincial rights, that he had been here for fourteen years and had never heard that they cared for provincial governments or had any regard or respect for them. He did not say that those better men of his own party and of our party established provincial rights in this country together. He did not say that the speeches that were made by many all down through the years on both sides of the house indicated a belief in provincial rights.
I was somewhat amused when in the course of his speech he was critical of the leader of this party. I would ask the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) to make a note of this page.

I will read the lines to the minister, and I think he will be able to And them on that page. I do not want to take undue advantage of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in his absence, although he could not change the language today if he were here. He says, at page 785 of Hansard:
Under the system that is being followed now it is true that we centralize criticism upon the federal government, but when the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) gets up and says that is centralizing government in Canada, I say to him that what we are actually doing is allowing the provincial governments to spend enough money to make themselves popular and keep themselves in power.
That was when he was waxing eloquent about provincial rights. Now at this late day in our confederation in Canada we have a great Liberal champion who will allow the provincial governments to spend enough money to keep them in power. It may not matter to him now whether they are Liberal or Conservative or if by chance they are represented by socialists. But the incident recalls to me the days when I sat in the house and heard the ex-Prime Minister say, not a five-cent piece to any Tory government.
I had intended to speak about centralization, but I am satisfied after hearing the returns from Digby-Annapolis-Kings and, again, the louder and more vociferous returns from Nicolet-Yamaska.

The Address-Mr. Rowe Mr. Rowe: The hon. member may laugh, but the laugh was the other way; and he who laughs last laughs best. I have seen this country divided and I have seen the olive branch of unity tossed hither and yon. But now at last we find that we have a common purpose in this country, and that no longer can there be raised those issues that should not be raised. If anyone here doubts me when I say that we must restore enterprise, safeguard our individual freedom and revive the national character, in view of the fact that we are one of the last outposts in the world, may I say that I know there are those to your right, Mr. Speaker, who believe the same thing. I will quote only some of the statements that have been made. The Hon. Angus L. Macdonald said:
. . . the present government has no life-lease on power: that the war psychology should be over; that unelected bureaucracy should no longer govern Canada; that provincial rights should be restored; that we should have nine happy provinces, instead of nine different countries.
Then that congenial, lovable character who has represented Quebec South for so many years and who is an ex-minister of the crown, the Hon. C. G. Power, said this:
Ministers of the crown must abandon the practice of abdicating their functions, their duties, and shouldering their responsibilities on the shoulders of those irresponsible boards, committees and commissions.
It is because we have departed from that doctrine that a large part of the unrest in our ranks has developed. Without the existence of an almost allpowerful bureaucracy it is unlikely we would have had budget by radio, restraint of trade by embargoes and prohibitions, bungling of freight rates, and a snarling of interprovincial affairs.
Of his party he said:
. . . they should be provincial-righters instead of dominion centralizers.
He did not say that they were, but he said that they should be. Then he went on to say also:
Our party has gone down to defeat in three provinces. This should be testimony enough without further comment.
The further comment, I would say, is in the loss since that time of three ridings in which that type of party muddling has gone down to defeat.
I wish to thank the house for the courtesy extended to me. Before it is too late, Mr. Speaker, I hope the party to your right will return to the ways they intended to take; because even in opposition in the future they will be better off if they act in such a way as to be truer to their former selves.
